SIGNAL: BOT SHOPPING IS ABOUT TO BREAK OUT IN A BIG WAY

What happened: ChatGPT can pay for things now. Last Friday, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet https://every.?ev_audience=free for a small group of U.S. Pro subscribers. You add your credit card, your Dot https://every.?ev_audience=free (ChatGPT’s personal agent) shops for you, and you approve each purchase with Face ID or a fingerprint. The purchase is made without the agent or the merchant ever seeing your card number.

Why it matters: Checkout has been a hurdle for shopping agents, often requiring your card details or an account with a saved payment method. Wallet lets you approve purchases while keeping your card details hidden. Now, the hard part is deciding what to let agents shop for. Although we haven’t yet tested ChatGPT Wallet, our team members have already had agents make purchases and process refunds for them, and they’re more comfortable handing off some aspects of shopping than others.

What it means: ChatGPT Wallet fixes paying, not picking. Let your agent handle purchases when you’d take the first reasonable option and it already knows what you have, and keep approving each one, for now, because even the best agents still get it wrong sometimes. Stores are adjusting, too.

In a new report https://every.?ev_audience=free, Andreessen Horowitz calls this the start of the “B2A” (business-to-agent) economy, where agents increasingly decide which products to use, which services to subscribe to, and where to spend money on our behalf. Agent browsing traffic grew eightfold between August and October, and Shopify reported that orders from AI-powered searches grew nearly 13-fold year over year in Q1.

https://every.?ev_audience=freeAgent traffic grew eightfold in two months. (Source: Human Security via Andreessen Horowitz.)




Some stores still keep bots out. For example, Amazon famously blocks Meta’s Muse agent https://every.?ev_audience=free. But a16z expects stores will soon “have to fight for bots’ business.” Mike tested what wins that fight https://every.?ev_audience=free with simulated AI shoppers: The same product sold to Claude Sonnet 4 percent of the time with hype copy written for humans and 97 percent of the time with copy written for AI shoppers. (The same goes for articles—see his guide to getting agents to recommend yours https://every.?ev_audience=free.) Expect shopping to split between stores that block agents and stores that write for them.

Try this: This week, give your agent (Dot, Muse, Grok Bot, Duet, etc.) one purchase where you’d take the first reasonable option, like a refill or a rebooking. If your agent is Grok Bot, start with Lauren Tan https://every.?ev_audience=free’s guide https://every.?ev_audience=free to automating with it. She’s one of the people who build it.

INSIDE EVERY

HOW OUR TEAM USES AGENTS TO SHOP, WHAT WE BUY, AND WHAT AGENTS WE USE

Everyone at Every has atheir own personal agent https://every.?ev_audience=free, whether that’s Dot, GrokBot, Instinct, or something elseoften from different providers. But when it comes to shopping, the team is much more split not just on choice of agent but on whatthe types of things they let the agent buy for them. If you’re wondering what’s actually safe to hand off, here’s what we trust agents to buy, where they still slip up, and which ones we use.

 * Head of video Randy Counsman’s assistant buys his groceries and places Amazon orders with a saved card (“YOLO”). When it comes to getting his order rightOn order accuracy, he says it’s “no worse than DoorDash/Uber Eats.”
 * Head of operations Arielle Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free has her Dot fill an Amazon cart for the office grocery run, but she still checks it and presses buy herself: “I don’t 100% trust it.”
 * CEO Dan Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free’s agent had a rougher run. For a dinner he was cooking for his girlfriend, it bought salt and olive oil he already had, and frozen shrimp instead of fresh. “Basically still needs oversight in order to have common sense,” he says.

Tyler uses Grok Bot https://every.?ev_audience=free to call airlines and stores to change flights, upgrade seats, and get refunds.

 * Tyler says once you get Grok Bot logged into your accounts and trained on your preferences, it’s great for life admin.
 * For example, he lets it book his flights to Hilo, Hawaii, from Oahu, because “it’s a 45 minute flight where I spend more time at the airport than in the air.”
 * But he won’t let it pick a gift for his sister-in-law: “If you care at all about what that gift is, it’s going to be a slog.”
 * Why? Because if your purchase still depends on your taste and judgment, it takes time whether you or Grok Bot does the browsing.

But Grok Bot will often repeat the same mistakes, until you’ve typed the same instruction 10 times (in all caps), so for most people Tyler recommends Claude Duet https://every.?ev_audience=free, though he suspects he’s the only one at Every who prefers it to Dot. Fair warning: you should expect Duet to stop short of pressing the buy button fully autonomously for you.

What about you? Where do you let your agent buy, and where do you draw the line? Hit reply and tell us.

Getting teams to change how they work is a bigger obstacle than model capability. That was the message from Ode’s Hugh Wimberly, Anthropic’s Jeremy Hadfield, and Every head of platform Willie Williams https://every.?ev_audience=free at Thesis: 2027 https://every.?ev_audience=free.

The models are ready: Hadfield pointed to Bun, the software that runs Claude Code, whose 1 million lines of code were rewritten in Rust “fully autonomously in about a week,” followed by a few weeks of verification—a job that “literally would have taken a team over a year.”

The people side is slower. Wimberly’s advice is to automate the part of the job people don’t like first, then let them see it work. At one Ode client, 20-year veterans ignored the AI assistant until they watched new hires outpace them with it. Then, as Wimberly put it, “Oh, I have to keep up.”

Use it now: Pick the most time-consuming task your team already dislikes and automate that first. DISPATCHES FROM THE FRONTIER

OUR STAFF WRITER BUILT HER OWN WORD PROCESSOR

Pros really are making their own pro tools now. In August 2025, Katie Parrott https://every.?ev_audience=free published an essay about giving up on her first AI editor https://every.?ev_audience=free. It had been shaky from the start. While she built it during Think Week, it kept “rising and then collapsing like a soufflé.” At Every’s Demo Day for subscribers, she couldn’t get the AI part working, so she showed it with fake outputs and told the audience they were dummy content. After six weeks of debugging, she moved the work into a shared Claude project. Maintaining her own app wasn’t worth it.

This week, she introduced Wordbetter, a word processor with her Compound Writing https://every.?ev_audience=free skills built in, a home for your voice, style, and audience files, and comments where you can summon an AI writing coach for feedback on specific passages.

This time, the first feature request was dark mode. Katie asked her agent for it, and 17 minutes later, it returned a draft pull request.

Dan Shipper offered this discovery as a measure of progress: “You can judge AI progress by seeing which members of our team vibe code their own word processor.”

In 2022, building your own AI word processor took a builder like Nathan Baschez https://every.?ev_audience=free, who combined his engineering and design experience with GPT-3 to create Lex https://every.?ev_audience=free. By late 2025, Opus 4.5 https://every.?ev_audience=free had made it possible for founders like Dan to build ambitious software between running a company—leading to Proof https://every.?ev_audience=free, his editor for humans and AI agents to work on documents together. By 2026, we’ve reached the professional writer.

BTW: Kieran Klaassen built his own word processor, Everytype, with Fable 5.1, which we’d barely begun testing before Katie used 5.2 to create Wordbetter. Look out for more from Katie and Kieran on their competing word processors and what it means when anyone can build personalized software.
